accuracy.evidence: Checked against the EEF guidance report Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (2018/2021: plan, monitor, evaluate cycle), Flavell (1979) on metacognitive monitoring, Bjork, Dunlosky and Kornell (2013) on fluency illusions from re-reading, and Roediger and Karpicke (2006) on the testing effect. The fractions prerequisites are correct: adding fractions with different denominators uses equivalent fractions (England NC Year 5/6 fractions), and division facts for 7 are the inverse of the 7 times table.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented self-assessment errors: judging by familiarity after re-reading (Rana prediction, Ivy p1, challenge Q1), counting highlighting or a teacher's explanation as proof (challenge Q2, m1), rating a whole topic with one feeling (Kai's all-green map, Ben's I'm rubbish at fractions), revising solid parts because it feels good, attacking a gap before its shaky base, and treating a gap as permanent (challenge Q5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaggapmap is built on a whole-topic survey: proof cards dropped into solid, shaky and gap lanes, a six-tile fractions map that starts all green and is recoloured only by test results, prerequisite-ordering cards for three different maps, a fix-to-colour match and a four-stage gap-finding loop. Highest 6-token shingle overlap with another flagship lab is under 5%, and it differs from flagcalib (confidence calibration percentages) and flaglookback (reflection questions).

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers that feeling sure is not proof by testing Kai's map: all six tiles start green, and after testing only three stay solid, two are shaky and one is a gap. The priority step only accepts the base part (equivalent fractions, the 7 times table, the shaky area topic in tomorrow's test), and the match step makes each colour need a different fix rather than re-reading.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked first, each with a tempting wrong option: whether notes that felt easy after re-reading make a part solid (yes, it feels familiar), how many of Kai's six sure parts are solid (all 6), and whether re-reading everything is the best fix for every part. The lab then disproves each, and the done message names the prediction back.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with shuffled options; each wrong option has its own message, e.g. familiar is not the same as known; highlighting shows you read it, not that you can use it; the gap is built on equivalent fractions so the new work will not stick; with notes open and one slip it is shaky, not solid; everyone has gaps. Lab mislabels name the rule for the correct colour.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation reads at Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.7 and adult text at 7.4, inside the learner targets of 6.5 and 9.5 after the adult paragraphs were split into shorter sentences. Lab text uses three plain labels (solid, shaky, gap) defined once with a one-line rule each, and canvas prompts are a single sentence.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph states a rule or a concrete case: proof not feeling, the three colours and their tests, fix the base first, a fix per colour. No praise padding or throat-clearing; the explanation stays under the 12% overlap limit with every other lesson, including Knowing what you don't know and Reflecting After Learning.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px Android (light) and iPhone 13 (dark): the map switches to two columns, tested tiles show their result on two lines without clipping, label buttons sit below the map, and lane entries use short tags (3/3, no notes) so nothing overlaps. The loop diagram's centre caption was moved below the loop after it clipped; phone_sweep reports 0 findings.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13; axe-core finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme. Colour is never the only cue (every tile and lane carries the word Solid, Shaky or Gap), every canvas action has a labelled button twin (Test Mixed numbers, Mixed numbers is Shaky), and feedback goes to the polite live region and the canvas aria-label.

Roediger, H. L. and Karpicke, J. D. (2006) Test-enhanced learning, Psychological Science 17(3)
